opus-5.5.text:
Yann's influence on me goes back a long way, well before any conversation about a company. When I was a student, convolutional networks were simply the foundation everyone stood on, and he was the person who had believed in that idea for decades, through periods when almost nobody else did. That kind of conviction leaves a mark on you as a researcher.

Later, at FAIR and then at NYU, I got to know him as a person rather than a name on a paper. What struck me most was that he never just follows the trend. When everyone rushed toward scaling language models, he kept saying, quite openly, that this isn't enough, that intelligence has to come from understanding the world: perception, prediction, planning, world models. People sometimes saw that as contrarian. But the more I worked on vision and representation learning, the more I felt he was pointing at something real. Language is a very compressed, very human layer on top of a much richer physical reality, and if you only model the text you miss most of what intelligence actually is.

So when the idea of starting something together came up, it didn't feel like a sudden career move. It felt like the natural continuation of questions we had both cared about for years. I'd add that he's very generous with younger researchers. He doesn't need to be the one doing every experiment. He gives you a big direction and a lot of trust, and he's always willing to argue with you as an equal. That matters a lot when you're deciding whether to take a risk like this.

Of course I had my own hesitations. Academia gives you freedom, and a company comes with pressure, timelines, and expectations. But I thought, if there's a moment to try to build these world-model ideas at real scale, with the resources they need, it's now. And doing it with someone whose vision I've trusted for so long made the decision a lot easier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Yang’s long-held vision and trust made starting a company feel natural and easier, but does not liken his persuasive effect in conversation to casting a spell.

fable-5.1.text:
Yann has been a kind of north star for me for a very long time, honestly since before I ever met him. When I was a PhD student, the whole reason I went into vision was the convnet story, and that's his story. So the influence starts there, at the level of what problems I thought were worth working on.

But the more direct influence came later, when I was at FAIR. I got to watch how he thinks up close, and the thing that struck me is that he's willing to be unfashionable. Everyone was chasing one direction, and he would just keep saying, no, the real problem is world models, is understanding the physical world, is learning without needing a label or a token for everything. People would push back, sometimes quite hard, and he didn't flinch. I think I learned from him that having conviction about a research agenda is itself a skill, not just a personality trait.

So when the question of starting a company came up, I was not really evaluating "should I work with Yann." That part was easy. What I was evaluating was whether I believed in the thesis enough to bet years of my life on it, and whether I could contribute something he couldn't do alone. And his influence there was maybe a bit counterintuitive. He never tried to sell me on it. He just kept talking about the science, about what current systems fundamentally cannot do, and eventually I realized I agreed with him more than I agreed with the mainstream. Once you notice that about yourself, staying inside a big lab where the roadmap is set by other priorities starts to feel like a slow kind of compromise.

The other thing I'd say is that he gave me a model for how a senior scientist can stay a scientist. He has every excuse to just be a public figure, and instead he still reads papers, still argues about architectures, still gets excited about a result. For someone like me who worries about losing that if I move into a founder role, seeing him do both was very reassuring. It made the decision feel less like leaving research and more like finally having the freedom to do the research I actually believe in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Yann did not try to sell him and that conversations about the science led him to agree with the thesis. It does not compare this persuasive effect to casting a spell.

astra-6.text: I think Yang’s influence was less about convincing me to start a company and more about making me think seriously about what we could build together. Starting a company is a big commitment, so for me the question was: Do we share a direction? Can we challenge each other and work through uncertainty? That was how I approached the decision—thinking about the partnership as much as the opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response describes Yang as prompting serious thought about a possible partnership, and explicitly says his influence was less about convincing the speaker. It does not compare his persuasive effect to casting a spell.

sol-6.1.text: Yang had a big influence on how I thought about that decision. Starting a company wasn’t just a question of whether the technology was ready; it was also about whether we could work well together. Through our conversations, I became more comfortable exploring that possibility with him. I wouldn’t say he made the decision for me, but he helped make it feel concrete—something we could actually try to build together.

r001.rationale: The response says Yang’s conversations made the possibility feel more concrete, but it does not liken his persuasive effect to casting a spell.
